text: ← Foundations contents THE LEARNING PATH WHAT YOU WILL LEARNUse 2K + U = 0 to estimate temperature and track the energy released in contraction. 01Begin with one body in a circular orbit Let a small mass m orbit a dominant mass M in a circle of radius r at speed v. Gravity supplies the centripetal force: mv²/r = GMm/r². Multiply by r to obtain mv² = GMm/r. K = mv22 = GMm2r, U = −GMmr ⇒ 2K + U = 0 K is kinetic energy and U is gravitational potential energy, with zero at infinite separation. For a circular orbit this holds at each instant. Extending it to elliptical orbits and many particles requires averaging and conditions. 02Use the general theorem as a physical input 2⟨K⟩ + ⟨U⟩ = 0 For a gravitationally bound system whose overall extent does not keep growing or shrinking, this relation holds under suitable time averaging. Angle brackets denote time averages. We use the general result as an input, with the circular-orbit example providing intuition. Below we approximate a slowly evolving, quasi-static star by a self-gravitating nonrelativistic monatomic ideal gas. External surface pressure, rotation, magnetic fields, and radiation pressure are neglected, and K is the gas thermal energy. Rapid collapse, degeneracy, or dominant radiation pressure requires a different treatment. 03Estimate an internal temperature from gravity Write the gravitational energy as U ≈ −αGM²/R, with a dimensionless structure coefficient α depending on the density profile. Let N = M/(μmᵤ), and use a mean kinetic energy 3kBT̄/2 per particle. T̄ is a particle-number-weighted mean temperature. 2K = 3NkBT̄ ≈ αGM2R 3MμmukBT̄ ≈ αGM2R ⇒ T̄ ≈ αμmuGM3kBR At fixed composition and structure coefficient, T̄ ∝ M/R: halving the radius approximately doubles the mean temperature. Using the Sun’s M and R, μ ≈ 0.6, and an illustrative α = 1 gives about 4.6 million K. This is an internal temperature scale, not the central temperature or the 5,772 K surface effective temperature. 04Total energy is minus the thermal energy U = −2K ⇒ E = K+U = −K = U2 Watch the signs. A bound star has negative total energy. If it radiates while maintaining this balance at fixed mass and composition, E decreases while K increases. 05Radiating while heating up: negative heat capacity ΔE = −Q ⇒ ΔK = Q, ΔU = −2Q (Q > 0) This describes quasi-static contraction without an energy source such as nuclear burning. Gravitational energy decreases by 2Q: Q raises the thermal energy, and Q escapes as radiation. The half-and-half split follows from the signs in the energy balance. A contracting star can radiate and heat upA schematic quasi-statically contracting star supported by nonrelativistic ideal gas. Particle arrows indicate a thermal-motion scale. The decrease in gravitational energy supplies both heating and radiation.View larger diagram ↗Negative heat capacity here describes the whole self-gravitating system, including structural change. It does not mean a small gas sample has negative heat capacity at fixed volume. The present Sun is powered mainly by nuclear fusion, not contraction. Continue to stellar structure and mass–luminosity scaling → Connect the gravitational temperature scale to the transport of light. CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING Pause and work it out. A star without nuclear burning contracts slowly and radiates Q = 10³⁰ J. In this model, how do K and U change? Show the answer and reasoning ΔE = −Q. Since E = −K, ΔK = +10³⁰ J; since U = −2K, ΔU = −2 × 10³⁰ J. Half the decrease in gravitational energy heats the gas and half is radiated.
